overview: Torres Strait Islander communities maintain distinct island identities and traditions connecting sea, land, kinship and creative practice. Individual island histories cannot be reduced to one polity.

items.text: Alick Tipoti describes Octopus Clan dancing connected with particular moons and tides, followed by gathering octopus at low tide. His account links ceremony with ecological timing.
Traditional masks used turtle shell with materials such as pearl shell and feathers. Their making joined material knowledge with performance and ancestral stories.
Tipoti made Sugu Mawa in fibreglass in 2011, adapting the appearance of turtle shell for a large contemporary artwork. New materials support continuing cultural expression.
Tipoti draws on stories passed down by his father and elders, while also researching historical collections. Community knowledge and archival research contribute to his work.
The 1992 Mabo decision followed a case brought by Meriam people from Mer. It recognised their native title; this event is not a foundation date for Torres Strait Islander society.
The Torres Strait Regional Authority supports language preservation, art centres, cultural repatriation and the Gab Titui Cultural Centre. These activities sustain living community heritage.
